summary: Describes a private SIP header called P-Answer-State, used by the Open Mobile Alliance for Push to talk over Cellular. It indicates the answering mode of the handset and is meant only for that application. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Push to talk over cellular is a service where a button starts a call between several participants, and the caller wants to speak at once. This header lets the network signal that the called handset will probably answer by itself, so a server can answer the caller early.

subtitle: A private SIP header that lets push-to-talk servers say a handset will probably answer by itself, so the caller can start talking sooner.

tldr.problem: In Push to talk over Cellular the caller must be able to speak almost as soon as the button is pressed, but waiting for the called handset to answer, even automatically, adds delay.
tldr.mechanism: A PTT Server that has reason to think the called handset is in Automatic Answer mode adds a P-Answer-State header with the value Unconfirmed to a SIP response. Another PTT Server can then answer the caller and buffer the caller's media until a response marked Confirmed arrives.
tldr.outcome: The header is a private extension for the OMA PoC application only, and the RFC says its assumptions about network topology and transitive trust are generally not applicable in the Internet as a whole. It is Informational and has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4964 is an Informational RFC from September 2007. It provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and it has been updated by RFC 8996. The document limits its own applicability to the OMA PoC application, and says its assumptions about network topology and transitive trust are generally not applicable in the Internet as a whole.

sections.title: Push to Talk and Why Speed Matters
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Alliance is specifying the Push to talk Over Cellular (PoC) service, in which SIP is the protocol used to establish half-duplex media sessions across different participants. The service lets a SIP User Agent, the PoC terminal, establish a session to one or more other SIP User Agents at the same time, usually initiated by the initiating user pushing a button.

The alliance has defined a collection of very stringent requirements in support of the service. To give the user a satisfactory experience, the initial session establishment, from the time the user presses the button to the time they get an indication to speak, must be minimized. This document describes a private extension to address specific requirements of the PoC service and may not be applicable to the general Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Push to talk over cellular is a service where a button starts a half-duplex call between several participants. The caller has to speak as soon as possible after pressing the button, and this header is one way the network shortens that wait.

sections.title: Where This Extension Applies
sections.content:
The extension makes assumptions about network topology and about the existence of transitive trust, and the RFC states that these assumptions are generally not applicable in the Internet as a whole. The mechanism was designed to satisfy the requirements the alliance set for Push to talk over Cellular, for which either no general-purpose solution was found, where insufficient operational experience was available to understand whether a general solution is needed, or where a more general solution was not yet mature.

Section 6.3 lists the circumstances in which the header applies: networks where user agents engage in half-duplex communication, so the invited user cannot verbally acknowledge the answering of the session as in full-duplex communication; where the invited user agent can automatically accept the session without user intervention; where the network contains intermediate SIP servers that are trusted; where those servers know the current answer mode of the terminating user agent server and the media types and codecs likely to be accepted; where those servers can buffer media to reduce the time before the inviting user can send media; and where they assume knowledge of the network topology and of similar intermediate servers in the signalling path. Such configurations are generally not applicable to the Internet as a whole, where those trust relationships do not exist.
sections.plainLanguage: This works only where the servers in between are all known to each other and trusted. The open Internet has no such arrangement, so the header is meant for one kind of network.

sections.title: Answer Modes, PTT Servers and the New Terms
sections.content:
A PoC terminal can be configured in Automatic Answer mode, where it accepts session invitations immediately and plays out the media as soon as it is received, without the called user intervening. The user can alternatively configure the terminal to alert them first and require them to accept the invitation manually before media is accepted; this is Manual Answer mode. A terminal may support both modes or only one, and the user can change the setting often, perhaps because they are busy or are in a public place where they cannot use a speakerphone.

The alliance's PoC architecture uses PTT Servers within the network that can act as a conference focus, an RTP translator or a policy enforcement server. A PTT Server is a SIP network server that performs the network-based functions for the Push to talk service, and it can act as a SIP proxy or a back-to-back user agent depending on the functions it needs. There can be more than one PTT Server in a session.

The RFC introduces four terms. An Unconfirmed Indication is an indication that the final target user agent has yet to be contacted and an intermediate SIP node is saying it has information that hints the request is likely to be answered by the target. An Unconfirmed Response is a SIP 18x or 2xx response containing an Unconfirmed Indication. A Confirmed Indication is an indication that the target user agent has accepted the session invitation and is ready to receive media, and a Confirmed Response is a SIP 200 (OK) response containing a Confirmed Indication.
sections.plainLanguage: A handset can be set to answer an invitation by itself, or to alert its owner first. The PTT servers in the network often know which mode a handset is in, and this header lets them pass that hint along the signalling path.

sections.title: How the Header Is Used
sections.content:
The point of the extension is to let the network give a faster push to talk experience: an intermediate PTT Server provides a SIP 200 (OK) before the called user agent does, and buffers the media the caller sends so it can be replayed to the called user agent when it answers. Because the call is half-duplex and media bursts are short, typically in the order of 10 to 30 seconds, the additional end-to-end latency can be tolerated, and this considerably improves the user experience. The PTT Server can only do this when there is a high probability that the called user agent is in Automatic Answer mode, and PTT Servers near the called user agent are likely to have up-to-date knowledge of that answering mode. Because of the restricted bandwidth of the cellular network, they can pass that knowledge upstream faster than the called user agent can deliver an automatically generated SIP 200 (OK).

The flow runs like this. When a PTT Server forwards a SIP INVITE and knows the called user agent is likely to be in Automatic Answer mode, it also generates a SIP 183 provisional response with a P-Answer-State header field with the parameter Unconfirmed, to signal to upstream PTT Servers that they can buffer the caller's media. A PTT Server that wishes to buffer the caller's media, on seeing that provisional response, absorbs it and generates a SIP 200 (OK) with an appropriate answer for the caller's user agent. When the called user agent finally generates its own SIP 200 (OK), the PTT Server that sent the Unconfirmed provisional response adds a P-Answer-State header field with the parameter Confirmed; that response is absorbed by the buffering PTT Server, which has already sent a 200 (OK), and the buffering server starts playing out the buffered media.

The rules for reading the header are strict. A received SIP 18x response without a P-Answer-State header SHOULD NOT be treated as an Unconfirmed Response, and a SIP 18x carrying Confirmed MUST NOT be treated as a Confirmed Response, because that is an invalid condition. A SIP 200 (OK) without the header MUST be treated as a Confirmed Response. A PTT Server that buffers media SHOULD be prepared for the possibility of never receiving a Confirmed Response and SHOULD release the session if one does not arrive before the buffer overflows. The RFC also notes that it is not intended that multiple PTT Servers buffer serially.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that expects the handset to answer by itself sends a provisional response carrying the header with the value Unconfirmed. A server upstream then answers the caller straight away and holds the caller's media. When the real answer arrives, marked Confirmed, the held media is played out.

sections.title: Syntax, Proxy Behaviour and the Alternatives Rejected
sections.content:
The syntax is given in augmented Backus-Naur Form, with several definitions inherited from SIP. The header is a name, a colon, an answer type and any number of generic parameters, and the answer type is Confirmed, Unconfirmed, or a token.

A SIP proxy server does not need to understand the semantics of the header. As part of the regular SIP rules for unknown headers, a proxy forwards them. No Supported or Require headers are needed, because the sender of the header does not depend on the receiver understanding the extension; if the extension is not understood, the header is simply ignored. A PTT Server acting as a proxy may include Unconfirmed in an 18x response that it originates, and may add Confirmed to a Confirmed Response. The header is only included in a provisional response when the node sending it knows there is a PTT Server acting as a back-to-back user agent that understands the extension in the signalling path, and that server will only pass it on in a 200 (OK) or in the sipfrag of a NOTIFY. The originating user agent therefore only receives the header in a 200 (OK) or in the sipfrag of a NOTIFY.

Four other carriers for the same information were considered and rejected. A unique reason phrase in the 183 and 200 responses was rejected because reason phrases are normally intended for human readers and are not meant to be parsed by servers for syntactic and semantic meaning. A Reason header was rejected because that would be inconsistent with the intended use of the Reason header, its usage is not defined for these response codes, and it would have required registering a new protocol identifier. A feature tag in the returned Contact header was rejected because this is not a different feature but an attribute of the session, which can be applied to many different features. A new SDP attribute was rejected because the answer state applies to the session and not to a media stream. The P-Answer-State header was chosen so that, even though the user agent sees that its offer has been answered and accepted, it can tell whether the invited subscriber or just an intermediary accepted the INVITE.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries one word, Confirmed or Unconfirmed, and any number of generic parameters. A proxy that does not understand it forwards it anyway, because SIP says unknown headers are passed on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The information returned in the P-Answer-State header is not viewed as particularly sensitive. It is informational in nature, telling the calling user agent that delivery of any media sent as a result of an answer in that response is not guaranteed, and an eavesdropper cannot gain any useful information from the contents of the header.

End-to-end protection is not appropriate, because the header is used and added by proxies and intermediate user agents. A malicious proxy between the user agents, or an attacker on the signalling path, could add or remove the header or modify its contents. Such an attack either denies the caller the knowledge that the callee has yet to be contacted, or falsely indicates that the callee has yet to be contacted when they have already answered. The second attack could lead the caller to decide not to transmit media, because they do not wish to have their media stored by an intermediary, even though in reality the callee has answered; the first does not appear to be a significant concern, since it is the same situation as a back-to-back user agent sending a 200 (OK) before the callee has answered without the use of this extension.

It is therefore necessary to protect the messages between proxies, and implementations SHOULD use a transport that provides integrity and confidentiality between the signalling hops. TLS-based signalling in SIP can provide this protection. The RFC closes by saying that security issues have only been considered for networks that are trusted and use hop-by-hop security mechanisms with transitive trust, and that security issues with usage of this mechanism in the general Internet have not been evaluated.
sections.plainLanguage: Because proxies add and use this header, it cannot be protected end to end. A proxy or an attacker on the signalling path could change it, so the signalling between hops should be protected with TLS.

data.title: ABNF
data.code:
P-Answer-State = "P-Answer-State" HCOLON answer-type
                 *(SEMI generic-param)
answer-type = "Confirmed" / "Unconfirmed" / token
